ff5884d7ac: The four great forms of Chinese verse, and modern poetry
f77dee254f: Ge and xing, with no limit on characters or lines, mostly five or seven characters per line
4fc51c8b4a: Regulated verse: quatrains and eight-line poems, with a fixed number of characters
8df3957e2d: Short, medium and long tunes, with uneven line lengths
19ad316d50: Sanqu and opera songs, with set line patterns that allow extra filler characters
e49236a40c: No limits on form or rhyme
7b0ac3ef03: Yuefu, ancient-style poems, regulated verse and modern poetry
96a692bd8f: No limit, mainly five or seven per line
c27c4a5cfc: No limit, mostly five or seven
df77397f0c: Even lines rhyme, one rhyme throughout
73eddba785: The middle two couplets are parallel
73c0d8e9f3: The stricter the metre, the more refined the words, but not necessarily the more singable. Pop lyrics sit between poetry and speech: they keep the rhythm, and they keep the naturalness of talk.
3836682001: Some change rhyme, some keep one rhyme
1522f75dfe: One rhyme throughout, all four tones may rhyme
a52b947847: Follows the ci pattern, no filler characters
c9db661782: Carried on the spirit of Han and Wei yuefu, absorbed the influence of music from the northern peoples, and grew out of folk song. Ci could be called poetry set free, with no limit on characters or lines.
235a638cd9: A new form from the Jin and Yuan dynasties onward, evolved from ci. It blended the street songs of the north with foreign tunes, combining metre and freedom.
593c836739: BuildWhat poems, ci and qu are like
031adbd2d7: Seeing classical verse again in the language of pop music
ad52d84921: Strict metre, careful about parallelism and paired lines, with less thought for singability.
8420aee3e7: Loose form, allowing changes in characters and lines. It's written much like "writing lyrics" in pop.
7a13b9d505: Inherits the form of ci and adds filler characters, making it the most singable. It's written much like "setting lyrics" in pop.
44cd2278d4: A standalone song that can be released on its own.
9443e60c38: Several songs strung into one complete story, like a concept album or a musical.
4b3264d2a5: Which form allows filler characters in its lines and is the most singable?
0021faa262: Yuan qu inherits the form of ci and also allows filler characters, so its lines are more flexible.
3b194ead6c: How many characters are in a seven-character quatrain?
61a76014cc: A quatrain has four lines of seven characters, 28 in all; a seven-character regulated poem has eight lines, 56 in all.
d5b6fbc8f9: Writing lyrics makes standalone words; setting lyrics makes words for a tune
5e3f682395: Written following a pop song's form
c2dcc995a2: The words can be read on their own and aren't necessarily singable
234ebf0634: Groove and sound need extra thought when the music is written
00cec834e9: Written following the form and sounds, making it more singable
06cb1f9c1d: Takes the melody's contour and pitch into account to reduce clashes between words and music
6ee6d69582: Placing the hook is key, echoing the title where needed
b02a6560a8: Your song will use both: today and next lesson you write lyrics first, then after setting music in Lessons 5 and 6 you go back and revise the words to the melody, which is setting lyrics.
4b7eb6527b: Mandarin has four tones, and the melody should follow each character's direction
76b7257099: When the melody moves against a character's tone, listeners easily misunderstand. Put 「淚」 (4th tone, "tears") on a rising melody, for instance, and it's easily heard as 「雷」 (2nd tone, "thunder").

51ed463ea4: Speak the lyrics first, then hum the melody, and compare which way each goes. Words on long notes and strong beats matter most; try to make their tones match the melody.

54ea27cb76: "I" speaks directly. It moves people most easily and is the most common view in pop lyrics.
cfe8a93933: Speaking to "you", like a letter; the 「寫信告訴我」 ("write and tell me") of 〈聽海〉 uses this voice.
659fc168e0: An onlooker tells "his" or "her" story, keeping a distance and leaving room for the listener's imagination.
584665f7d2: Don't waver: if the person and stance keep changing within one song, listeners can't find who's speaking. The planning card for 〈十年〉 reads "first-person stance, telling a story in first, second and third person": the speaker is always "I".
